column3: The Hebrew calls his condition sickness and says that he became ill; BSB uses injury and says that he injured himself.
The Hebrew explicitly commands him to arise as well as go up.
The Hebrew describes going up onto the bed and not coming down from it; BSB describes lying on it and not getting up.
The Hebrew leaves the recipient unnamed; BSB calls him the king.
The Hebrew does not separately specify “these men” and describes going up onto the bed and not coming down from it.
The Hebrew leaves the speaker unnamed; BSB calls him the king.
The Hebrew leaves the final speaker unnamed; BSB calls him the king.
The Hebrew leaves the sender and recipient unnamed; BSB supplies King Ahaziah and Elijah.
The Hebrew ends with “him”; BSB specifies the captain.
The Hebrew leaves the sender and recipient unnamed and explicitly mentions answering; BSB supplies the king and Elijah.
The Hebrew says Elijah spoke “to them,” in the plural, and ends with “him,” where BSB specifies the captain.
The Hebrew has singular “soul” for his own life and singular “soul” for the fifty servants; BSB uses plural “lives” for the servants.
The Hebrew leaves speaker and recipient unnamed and places the sending of messengers before its question about God. BSB names Elijah and King Ahaziah.
The Hebrew leaves the deceased unnamed; BSB supplies Ahaziah.
